member.summary:
Molar mass of dry air used to define the specific gravity (relative density) of a gas, γ = M_gas / M_air (ideal-gas definition).
There is no single value: each standard or textbook fixes its own, and the choice changes γ by up to 0.14 %. The engine never picks one silently; the caller passes the reference that matches the source of its data.

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Thermodynamics.StandingPseudoCriticalCorrelation
member.summary:
Standing (1977) pseudo-critical curves, field units (°R, psia), for hydrocarbon gas without non-hydrocarbons (apply or for CO₂, H₂S, N₂).
Sources disagree on the dry-gas Ppc intercept (667 or 677 psia, 1.5 % in Ppc); makes the choice explicit. The condensate curve is the same in both (Ppc slope −51.7: Ppc must fall as the gas gets heavier). Whitson & Brulé recommend the dry-gas curve for γ ≤ 0.75 and the condensate curve above; follows that.

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Thermodynamics.WichertAzizCorrection
member.summary: Wichert & Aziz (1972) correction of pseudo-critical properties for sour gas (field units, as published): A = y_CO₂ + y_H₂S, B = y_H₂S ε [°R] = 120·(A^0.9 − A^1.6) + 15·(B^0.5 − B^4) T'pc = Tpc − ε P'pc = Ppc · T'pc / (Tpc + B·(1 − B)·ε) Reported range: y_CO₂ < 0.544, y_H₂S < 0.738. Never applied implicitly: the caller decides whether the gas needs it.

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Thermodynamics.PseudoCriticalProperties
member.summary:
Pseudo-critical temperature and pressure of a gas, the reducing parameters of the corresponding-states Z correlations (Tpr = T / Tpc, Ppr = P / Ppc).
They are not the true critical point of the mixture: they are whatever values make the generalized Z chart (Standing–Katz) fit the gas. Where they come from is a modelling choice and must be stated by the caller: - : mole-fraction average of the component critical properties (Kay 1936), when the composition is known; - : from specific gravity (Sutton, Standing), when only γ is known; - : adjustment for CO₂ and H₂S.

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Thermodynamics.Aga8DetailModel
member.summary:
AGA Report No. 8 Part 1, DETAIL characterization equation of state (AGA8-DC92; ISO 12213-2) — the reference equation for the compression factor of natural gas in transmission and custody transfer.
Port of the NIST reference implementation (E. W. Lemmon, I. H. Bell, usnistgov/AGA8, AGA8CODE/C/Detail.cpp, version 2.0, 2017); the NIST code is not subject to copyright in the United States and its notice permits use, modification and redistribution. Constants, units (kPa, mol/L, K, R = 8.31451) and algorithms are kept as in the original; only the global state was replaced by an immutable, thread-safe instance per composition.
Uncertainty stated by AGA for the normal range (≈ 265–335 K, ≤ 12 MPa, pipeline-quality gas): about 0.1 % in Z. Outside the normal range the equation is still evaluated; the caller warns. The normal range has two independent parts, checked separately so one cause gives one warning: pressure and temperature (, called at every point) and composition (, a property of the gas, checked once by whoever defines the fluid).

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Thermodynamics.CngaCompressibilityModel
member.summary:
California Natural Gas Association (CNGA) correlation, explicit, as given by Menon, Gas Pipeline Hydraulics (Eq. 1.12):
Z = 1 / (1 + Pg · 344400 · 10^(1.785·G) / Tf^3.825)
Pg gauge pressure, psig Tf temperature, °R G gas specific gravity (air = 1)
The formula works with GAUGE pressure, so the atmospheric pressure is an explicit input (no silent 14.7 psia). Menon states it is valid for Pg > 100 psig and takes Z = 1 below; this implementation always evaluates the formula (Z → 1 smoothly as Pg → 0, with no jump at 100 psig) and reports Pg ≤ 100 psig as outside the validated range.
A candidate for the "PCS (closed-form)" Z option of the original GTHPS program, together with ; the report does not say which one it used.

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Thermodynamics.DranchukAbouKassemModel
member.summary:
Dranchuk & Abou-Kassem (1975): 11-constant fit of the Standing–Katz chart (Benedict-Webb-Rubin form), solved for the reduced density ρr = 0.27·Ppr / (Z·Tpr):
Z = 1 + (A1 + A2/Tr + A3/Tr³ + A4/Tr⁴ + A5/Tr⁵)·ρr + (A6 + A7/Tr + A8/Tr²)·ρr² − A9·(A7/Tr + A8/Tr²)·ρr⁵ + A10·(1 + A11·ρr²)·(ρr²/Tr³)·exp(−A11·ρr²)
Validated range: 1.0 ≤ Tpr ≤ 3.0, 0.2 ≤ Ppr ≤ 30. Inside that range the equation has exactly one root in 0 < ρr ≤ 3 (checked on an 81 × 150 grid, largest root 2.46), found by Brent's method. Measured against NIST (pure methane/nitrogen, Kay pseudo-criticals = true criticals): see CorrespondingStatesAccuracyTests.

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Thermodynamics.HallYarboroughModel
member.summary:
Hall & Yarborough (1973): Starling-Carnahan form fitted to the Standing–Katz chart, solved for the reduced density parameter y:
t = 1/Tpr 0 = −A·Ppr + (y + y² + y³ − y⁴)/(1 − y)³ − B·y² + C·y^D A = 0.06125·t·exp(−1.2·(1 − t)²) B = t·(14.76 − 9.76·t + 4.58·t²) C = t·(90.7 − 242.2·t + 42.4·t²) D = 2.18 + 2.82·t Z = A·Ppr / y
Validated range, as usually reported: 1.15 ≤ Tpr ≤ 3.0, 0.2 ≤ Ppr ≤ 20.5. Below Tpr ≈ 1.15 it departs from DAK by up to 12 % (measured at Tpr 1.05). The equation has one root in 0 < y < 1 over 1 ≤ Tpr ≤ 3, 0.2 ≤ Ppr ≤ 30 (checked on an 81 × 150 grid; largest root y = 0.55), found by Brent's method.

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Thermodynamics.PapayModel
member.summary:
Papay (1968), explicit: Z = 1 − 3.53·Ppr / 10^(0.9813·Tpr) + 0.274·Ppr² / 10^(0.8157·Tpr)
Closed form, no iteration. The sources consulted give no validity range. The range declared here is where Papay stays within (5 %) of DAK, the reference fit of the same chart. That region is not a rectangle: the largest acceptable Ppr grows from 0.53 at Tpr 1.0 to 7.45 at Tpr 1.4 and beyond, so it is tabulated every 0.05 in Tpr (), each node rounded down to 0.01 and the lower of the two neighbouring nodes used in between. Scanned for Ppr ≤ 15. Dense check (401 × 300 points inside the region, 2026-10-04): largest deviation 4.998 %.

member.name: T:NaturalGasPipeline.Thermodynamics.LeeGonzalezEakinViscosityModel
member.summary:
Lee, Gonzalez & Eakin (1966), "The Viscosity of Natural Gases", J. Pet. Technol. 18(8), 997-1000.
μ [cP] = 1e-4 · K · exp(X · ρ^Y) K = (9.4 + 0.02·M) · T^1.5 / (209 + 19·M + T) X = 3.5 + 986 / T + 0.01·M Y = 2.4 − 0.2·X with T in °R, M in g/mol and ρ in g/cm³ (the correlation's own units; the conversion is done here, explicitly, and nowhere else).
Applicability: hydrocarbon natural gases. Measured against NIST (methane, 273–313 K, 1–10 MPa) it over-predicts by +1.2 % to +4.1 %. It is NOT valid for non-hydrocarbon gases: for pure nitrogen it is off by about −45 %. Gases with a large N₂/CO₂/H₂S content need a correction (e.g. Carr–Kobayashi–Burrows) or a different model.

member.summary: Used to indicate to the compiler that a method should be called in its containing module's initializer.
member.remarks:
When one or more valid methods with this attribute are found in a compilation, the compiler will emit a module initializer which calls each of the attributed methods.
Certain requirements are imposed on any method targeted with this attribute: - The method must be `static`. - The method must be an ordinary member method, as opposed to a property accessor, constructor, local function, etc. - The method must be parameterless. - The method must return `void`. - The method must not be generic or be contained in a generic type. - The method's effective accessibility must be `internal` or `public`.
The specification for module initializers in the .NET runtime can be found here: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/design/specs/Ecma-335-Augments.md#module-initializer
